newsitem.title: INDIA: Tight margins seen hitting India Grasim profits.
newsitem.headline: Tight margins seen hitting India Grasim profits.

text.p: Pressure on margins and lower income from shrinking cash surpluses will cut profits of India's diversified Grasim Industries for the year ended March 31, 1997, analysts said on Monday.
Grasim is India's largest producer of viscose staple fibre (VSF), a textile raw material. It also makes cement, sponge iron and textiles.

"Prices of all commodities that Grasim makes have been languishing," said Mahendra Datar, company analyst at Ceat Financial Services. "This is bound to hit profits even though there will be volumes' growth."
Analysts have forecast the net profit to fall 9.74 percent to 2.99 billion rupees in 1996/97 from 3.32 billion a year earlier, according to a Reuter poll consensus.
The flagship firm of Aditya Birla industrial group is scheduled to release its results on Wednesday.
Lower margins in VSF business, which accounts for 60 percent of Grasim's profits and 40 percent of its turnover, and cement would squeeze profits, analysts said.
"VSF prices have fallen 15-16 percent in 1996/97," said Ajay Jindal, analyst at Caspian Securities. "Broadly, profits should be down 10 percent."

Lower international prices and cheaper substitutes like cotton and polyester staple fibre were twin factors that hit VSF, but Grasim was able to partly offset the impact by a 40 percent drop in raw material costs, he said.
Electricty shortages and sluggish demand would have undermined capacity utilisation of its cement plants, analysts said, adding they saw little improvement in the near-term.
Analysts expect the firm's foray into sponge iron to bear fruit, after being beset by teething problems a year earlier.
Cash surpluses are expected to fall sharply wiping out other income, or earnings from investments other than its main businesses, analysts said.
"Other income will be substantially lower," said Gagan Gupta, analyst at Daewoo Securities. "It will drag down the profits."

Other income is expected to more than halve to one billion rupees from 2.11 billion in 1995/96. This had fallen to 723.2 million rupees in the first half on 1996/97 from 1.13 billion in the same period a year ago.
Analysts saw little prospect of an upturn over the next two years. "We don't see substantial growth," said Caspian's Jindal. "The only volume growth is from VSF but we see over-supply."
Grasim is expected to commission a 60,000 tonnes per annum VSF plant in two stages in 1997/98, taking its total capacity to 240,000 tonnes.
Jindal forecast an earnings per share of 42 rupees in 1996/97 and 46 rupees in 1997/98 against 45.9 rupees in 1995/96.

Grasim raised $90 million and $100 million respectively in 1992 and 1994 through global depositary receipts issues overseas, but a third issue for $125 million had to be called off in 1996/97 due to poor market conditions.
